title: Much Ado About Nothing
author: William Shakespeare
openingText: [Enter Leonato, Hero, Beatrice and others, with a Messenger.]
about:
Two soldiers return from a successful campaign to the household of Leonato, governor of Messina. The young Count Claudio falls in love at first sight with Leonato's daughter Hero, and the wedding is arranged within hours. Claudio's older friend Benedick, a confirmed bachelor, falls into his usual sparring with Leonato's niece Beatrice, who has matched him insult for insult since they last met. Their friends decide, more or less for sport, to trick the two of them into believing the other is in love with them.

While this is going on, the bastard Don John — the villain of the play — tricks Claudio into believing he has seen Hero unfaithful at her bedroom window the night before her wedding. Claudio denounces her at the altar; her family pretends she is dead. The watch — Shakespeare's most famous comic constables — stumbles onto the conspiracy and finds out the truth almost by accident. Claudio repents, Hero is revealed alive, both couples marry, and Benedick orders the music to strike up.

Much Ado was first performed around 1599, the same year as Henry V and As You Like It, in the very middle of Shakespeare's career. It is the play in which he perfected the romantic comedy of wit, the form a thousand later comedies have copied — most directly, every story in which two people who hate each other on sight end up married by the end.

angleCards.title: Beatrice and Benedick.
angleCards.text: They are the model for every screwball couple in the four hundred years since: two clever people who insult each other until they discover, often by being tricked, that the insults were a way of paying attention.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Beatrice and Benedick as the original screwball couple — how their sparring works, what their friends do to them, and what Shakespeare thinks love between equals looks like.

angleCards.title: What happens to Hero.
angleCards.text: The other plot is darker. Hero is publicly accused of unchastity at her own wedding by the man who said he loved her yesterday. The play turns into something close to tragedy, then turns back. Watch what it takes to put her back together.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Hero's plot — the slander at the altar, her family's response, and what the play asks of her after Claudio has wronged her — as the darker half of the comedy.

angleCards.title: The men in love.
angleCards.text: Claudio falls in love at first sight, accepts the slander at face value, denounces his fiancée in church, and is forgiven by the end. Benedick takes longer at every step. The play is the comparison between them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare Claudio's love and Benedick's love side by side — what each man takes for granted, what he is willing to believe, and which one the play prefers.

angleCards.title: Dogberry and the watch.
angleCards.text: The play is rescued from disaster by an officious, malapropping night watchman who blunders into the truth without understanding it. Dogberry is one of Shakespeare's best comic creations and the engine of the plot's resolution.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Dogberry and the watch as more than comic relief: how Shakespeare makes a self-important fool the only character who can save the play.

cast.name: Beatrice
cast.description: Sharp-tongued, fast, refusing to marry, in mourning for some unspecified history with Benedick. She has more wit per line than anyone else in the play and is the model for several centuries of later heroines who say what they think and mean it.

cast.name: Benedick
cast.description: A young lord of Padua, lately returned from the wars, a sworn bachelor and a relentless joker. He has been crossing swords with Beatrice for years. His friends decide to convince him she is dying of love for him, and the joke takes.

cast.name: Claudio
cast.description: A young soldier in Don Pedro's company, in love with Hero from the moment he sees her. He is brave on the field and credulous off it. He will believe what he is told about Hero and denounce her at the altar.

cast.name: Hero
cast.description: Leonato's only child, quiet, dutiful, and devoted to Claudio. She has nothing like her cousin Beatrice's tongue. The play's worst scenes happen to her, and she comes back to life — formally and almost literally — at the end.

cast.name: Don Pedro
cast.description: The visiting prince whose military success has brought everyone to Messina. He arranges Claudio's match, plans the Beatrice–Benedick trick, and presides over the comedy from a slight distance. He is the unmarried friend who matchmakes everyone else and ends the play alone.

cast.name: Don John
cast.description: Don Pedro's illegitimate brother, recently defeated and reconciled, a born malcontent who will spoil what he can. He stages the trick at Hero's window for no clearly stated reason beyond the pleasure of ruining other people's happiness. He is Iago in miniature.

acclaim.quote: Heart of my heart, I will not, but I love thee none the worse for it.
acclaim.context: letter to John Forster, 1844, on Beatrice and Benedick

acclaim.quote: Perhaps no play of Shakespeare contains more humour and serious matter so well intermingled.

whyItMatters.title: The Original Romantic Comedy
whyItMatters.body: Almost every romantic comedy made since the 1930s — His Girl Friday, The Philadelphia Story, When Harry Met Sally, You've Got Mail, Pride and Prejudice in its film and television lives — owes a direct debt to Much Ado About Nothing. Two clever people who appear to hate each other; a friend group that engineers their courtship; a plot that turns on misunderstandings the characters could clear up if they would only speak. Shakespeare did not invent this shape, but he gave it its first fully convincing English form, with two leads sharp enough that they have stayed in repertory for four centuries. Beatrice and Benedick's verbal duels are the source of the entire later tradition of the screwball couple — the pair who get the best lines in every scene and end up together because no one else in the play can keep up with either of them.

whyItMatters.title: The Comedy That Brushes Against Tragedy
whyItMatters.body: Much Ado is built like a comedy, with two weddings and a dance at the end, but its central plot is much darker than the form suggests. Hero is slandered by her fiancé on the morning of their wedding in front of her father, her cousin, her household, and the prince of Aragon. Claudio not only refuses to marry her but accuses her of being unchaste in language designed to humiliate; Leonato joins in. She faints and is reported dead. Friar Francis, in one of the few quiet, serious speeches of the play, talks the family into pretending the report is true and waiting. Benedick — until then the comic relief — is asked by Beatrice to kill Claudio, and he says yes. For three scenes the play stops being a comedy at all. Then Dogberry's watchmen stumble in with the truth and the play recovers. The recovery is real, but the wound the play opens up in the middle is also real, and the marriage at the end is a marriage to a man who, last Tuesday, called his fiancée a whore in church.

whyItMatters.title: The Fool Who Knows Without Knowing
whyItMatters.body: Dogberry, the constable of the watch, is the most quoted comic character in the play and one of the two or three best in Shakespeare. He gives orders his deputies cannot understand. He uses long words wrong. He insists on being recorded as an ass. He is also — and this is what makes the comedy work — the only character in the entire play who actually solves the central problem. While the heroes and heroines are tying themselves into knots over honour, slander, and revenge, Dogberry's incompetent watch catches the villains in the act, holds them overnight, and delivers them to the authorities, mostly by following orders that nobody else thought were worth giving. Shakespeare is making a joke about institutions: the comic, despised, half-corrupt machinery of the law works while everyone else is too busy with their own dignity to notice. It is the same joke he tells about the gravediggers in Hamlet and the porter in Macbeth, and Much Ado is where he tells it best.
